editorial.headline: Specialist Livestock Retail: Nationally Open, Barred for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This specialist retail activity is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent moratorium blocks PMA registration.
editorial.body:
At its core, this is specialist retail trade in livestock products: milk, eggs, livestock meat and poultry meat. It is a retail activity defined by those goods rather than a broad description of food commerce. That specificity matters because the registration question starts with what is sold. For an operator centred on the retail sale of these farming outputs, the activity sits within the stated scope.

Registration is open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar business scales. At the national level, its PMA status is open, with a maximum foreign-ownership figure of 100%. That makes for a straightforward national reading: foreign capital may hold the full stake within the recorded national ceiling. The figure is supported by Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021; it is not a promise that the same registration can proceed in every locality. That distinction determines the Bali outcome.

In Bali, the answer changes decisively. A foreigner cannot register this activity as PMA in Bali today. The record marks it as blocked by risk class: at the Besar scale, the OSS risk classification is Low or Medium-Low across every stated scope. That places the activity within Bali’s moratorium, in force from May 2026. The provincial rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI from PMA on an island-wide, permanent basis. It is therefore misleading to treat national openness as a Bali operating clearance. The national 100% ceiling remains the national ceiling; it does not displace the Bali block.

For founders, the conclusion is short but not simplistic. The activity’s commercial identity is specific—retailing milk, eggs, livestock meat and poultry meat—and its available scales are broad. Nationally, it is open to PMA with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. In Bali, however, the permanent moratorium blocks PMA registration because of the recorded risk classification at the Besar scale. The useful question is not whether the activity is nationally open in the abstract, but whether it can be registered as PMA in the place where it will operate. Here, today’s Bali answer is no.
